Abstract.
All RLWE-based FHE schemes are inherently noisy. The CKKS scheme
(Cheon, Kim, Kim, Song, Asiacrypt 2017) considers the noise as a part of the message,
yielding approximate computations but also considerable performance gains. Since it
grows with each homomorphic operation and incurs a precision loss, it is paramount
for users to be able to estimate the noise level throughout a given circuit in order to
appropriately estimate parameters and control the precision loss in the message. In
this work, we develop a noise model that allows for tight estimates of the precision
loss, and propose a tool prototype for computing these estimates on any given circuit.
Our noise model relies on a novel definition, the component-wise noise, which makes
the average-case noise estimates tighter and more composable. As a result, our model
and tool can derive accurate estimates of complex circuits such as bootstrapping.
We experimentally demonstrate the tightness of our noise estimates by showing that
our theoretical estimates never deviate by more than 0.01 bits from experimental
estimates, even for large circuits, and hold with high probability. Furthermore, we
demonstrate how to apply our techniques to obtain an exact version of the CKKS
scheme in which the decryption removes all the noise (with high probability). Such
a scheme has many applications, as it allows to take advantage of the efficiency of
CKKS, while preserving an exact message space, hence further strengthening CKKS
against IND-CPA-D attacks.

Introduction
Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables meaningful computations on encrypted
data. Following Gentry’s initial construction from standard lattice assumptions, current
constructions [BGV12, CKKS17, CGGI20, DM15, FV12, GSW13] are based on variants
of the Learning-with-Error problem (LWE) [Reg09]; improving their efficiency has been a
significant endeavor of the field. The cornerstone of efficiency is to manage noise: a small
random deviation added for security purposes during the encryption process which grows
throughout the computation and which must be filtered out during decryption. Hence,
the correctness of current FHE schemes depends on successful message decoding and is
therefore probabilistic.

Noise Estimates for CKKS
One of the most popular schemes to date for computing on approximate real and
complex numbers was introduced by Cheon et al. [CKKS17] and is dubbed CKKS. Its
efficiency stems from a simple noise management strategy: it considers the error as part of
the approximation error of its underlying plaintext, resulting in an approximate scheme.
That is, instead of returning the plaintext pt, the decryption algorithm returns pt+e, where
e is a small noise term – no attempts are made to separate the noise from the plaintext. This
is different in so-called exact FHE schemes ([BGV12, CGGI20, DM15, FV12, GSW13]).
These apply more advanced encoding strategies to make sure that the noise can be
completely removed during decryption: BGV [BGV12] scales the noise e with the plaintext
modulus t. This leads to the noise always being a multiple of the plaintext modulus, as long
as it does not wrap around the ciphertext modulus. Thus, a reduction modulo the plaintext
modulus completely removes the noise, and the decryption algorithm only returns the
plaintext pt. In BFV, the message is scaled so that the noise is encoded in the lower bits,
allowing it to be rounded off as long as it remains below a certain bound. These techniques
enable exact decryption with a high probability, but result in a performance loss compared
to CKKS. In CKKS, the noise e is considered part of the plaintext and is not removed.
Thus, CKKS suffers from what is called precision loss: the more operations are performed
on ciphertexts, the more the noise e will grow, slowly polluting the least significant bits of
the message, and reducing the number of message bits that are returned exactly. Moreover,
it has been shown that an adversary with access to the raw decryption error through
decryption can mount passive key-recovery attacks [LM21]. Such attacks are captured by
the so-called IND-CPA-D model, and all countermeasures known to date require the user
to compute a bound on the decryption error. Therefore, for both correctness and security
reasons, it is essential for users to quantify this precision loss/noise growth throughout a
computation.
1.1
Our Contributions
Our contributions in this work are as follows. First, we present noise estimates for all
homomorphic operations in CKKS. Based on these estimates, we propose a tool, dubbed
the estimator, that can estimate the noise incurred by the evaluation of any circuit in
CKKS before runtime. Secondly, we make progress towards achieving IND-CPA-D security
for CKKS. We show how to use our noise estimates to obtain an exact version of the
CKKS scheme with some high probability δ. We call this scheme δ-exact CKKS.
In more detail, our contributions are as follows.
• Composable Average-Case Noise Bounds: We extend the existing work on average-
case noise analysis by (1) proposing a novel component-wise noise approach to
track the noise and (2) supporting plaintext-ciphertext operations, rotations and
conjugations. Thanks to these extensions, we can derive bounds on complex circuits
such as iterative algorithms or bootstrapping, which were left unaddressed by previous
works. We additionally present noise estimates for all the operations needed in
bootstrapping, such as homomorphic matrix-ciphertext products, encoding and
decoding. We experimentally confirm that our bounds are tight: they do not deviate
from the experimentally observed noise by more than 0.01 bits in all experiments.
• Open-Source Average-Case Noise Estimator: We provide a proof-of-concept open-
source estimator1 that calculates these noise bounds for any circuit. To do so, the
estimator simulates the noise at every step of the circuit. For input gates, this is
done by drawing fresh values according to the (user-provided) plaintext distribution.
For the arithmetic gates, this is done by sampling the noise distribution, according
to our composable bounds. Note that this can be done at circuit design time, i.e.,

schemes are trivially secure in this model. However, we could not prove IND-CPA-D
security for this version of CKKS. This is because our noise estimates rely on two
heuristics (commonly used in the literature [CCH+23, CNP23, BMCM23, MP24]: (1)
that all the noise terms are independent, and (2) that they are distributed according
to a Gaussian distribution. Indeed, while the noise distribution is well approximated
by a Gaussian (we verify this experimentally), we cannot formally quantify “how
close” it is to one, which would be required to prove full IND-CPA-D security.
1.2
Related Work
1.2.1
Noise analysis for CKKS
Costache et al. [CCH+23] provided the first average-case noise analysis for CKKS. They
developed noise estimates for encoding, encryption, addition, multiplication, relinearization,
and rescaling for both CKKS and RNS-CKKS [CHK+19]. We go further than the noise
estimates given in [CCH+23], as we also perform noise analysis for addition and multipli-
cation by plaintexts and constants, rotations, conjugations, and key-switchings in general.
We use a different approach, tracking the component-wise noise (Definition 2), instead of
the precision loss directly. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our noise estimates can be
combined into estimates for deep circuits such as bootstrapping and provide experimental
validation.
1.2.2
“Exact” CKKS
In the full version of their paper [CCH+22], Costache et al. also formalize the approach of
exact CKKS by rounding off the noise bits in the element pt + e output by the decryption
algorithm. However, they do not fully achieve an exact CKKS scheme, since they assume
circuits to be “correctable” in their proof; how circuits can be made correctable was left as
an open problem. We extend their work by showing how to obtain correctable circuits.
A different and recent topic of interest has been how to remove a certain part of the noise
in CKKS. The motivation for this approach is that the noise growth in CKKS means that
only circuits of limited depth can be meaningfully evaluated, since the noise eventually will
swallow the message (unless the circuit benefits from self-correcting properties). Drucker
et al. [DMPS24] propose a method to reduce the error of a CKKS ciphertext encrypting
binary values via the homomorphic evaluation of a step function. This keeps the error small
enough such that circuits of arbitrary depth, over this plaintext space, can be evaluated.
But this work seeks a different goal than ours: [DMPS24] focuses on the ability to evaluate
circuits of unlimited depth over binary values, whereas our work is focused on achieving
exactness over rationals of some fixed precision.
Bae et al. [BCKS24] build on the work by Drucker et al. [DMPS24] and propose new
bootstrapping algorithms that reduce the noise in CKKS ciphertexts encrypting binary
values, similar to bootstrapping in schemes such as BGV, BFV, and TFHE. Two follow-up
papers [BKSS25, AKP24] address some of the remaining open problems, including the

1.2.3
On average-case noise analysis
A recent work [GZ25] calls the average-case approach into question. In this paper, the
authors make a valid critique on how common heuristic assumptions are necessary for
average-case analyses (such as ours) to function. In more detail, the authors investigate
the validity of common heuristics, including those that we rely on: that the noise terms
are independent and follow a Gaussian distribution. Although the paper demonstrates
how these heuristics easily fail in corner cases, it also points out that such failure cases
did not lead to any decryption failure in practice for their case study (i.e., the OpenFHE
parameter selection tool). Hence, the conclusion from [GZ25] does not differ much from
ours: while such heuristics are not suitable to argue about the security of a scheme (this
prevents us from proving IND-CPA-D security for our version of exact CKKS), they still
enable precise noise analysis and meaningful applications in circuit design and parameter
selection.
1.2.4
Comparison with related work
We present a short comparison between our bounds and the bounds obtained in [CCH+23].
We find that for fresh ciphertexts, addition, and rescaling our bounds agree with the
bounds presented in [CCH+23]. However, while the bounds for multiplication presented
in [CCH+23] underestimate the experimentally observed noise by as much as 5 bits, our
bounds are tight (we observe a deviation from the theory of at most 0.01 bits. Additionally,
we consider many complex operations that [CCH+23] do not, and we also test our bounds
on large circuits (particularly, on deep circuit). Our bounds remain tight for large circuits,
which is not expected for [CCH+23], since their multiplication bounds underestimate the
experimentally observed noise.
Drucker et al. [DMPS24] also introduce an exact CKKS scheme. Their techniques
and targeted functionality, however, are very different from ours. Their approach aims at
providing SIMD gate bit-wise arithmetic, which they achieve by homomorphically applying
a step function after a number of gates have been evaluated, in order to maintain the noise
below some threshold. Recent works have extended the framework of Drucker et al. by
providing exact arithmetic over small integers [BCKS24, BKSS25, AKP24, Kim25], but
similarly to Drucker et al., the plaintext space remains small (e.g. 8 bits). Overall, these
works aim to provide the functionality of single ciphertext schemes (such as TFHE), but
with the efficiency and throughput of SIMD schemes. In contrast, we target SIMD exact
fixed point complex arithmetic over correctable circuits, and we achieve this by providing
very tight noise bounds for the given homomorphic circuit that is evaluated, which allows
us to remove the noise upon decryption. Finally, we note that our noise bounds have
applications beyond changing CKKS to be exact – for example, for determining appropriate
levels of noise-flooding for IND-CPA-D security [BCDS+25].

2.7
Average-case and Worst-case Noise Analysis
Two different approaches to track the noise in FHE schemes have been proposed: worst-
case noise analysis and average-case noise analysis. In a worst-case analysis, the noise
in the ciphertext is bounded at encryption and for each step of the computation. These
bounds are derived by assuming that the random variable falls within a certain number
of standard deviations (this number is selected to be α = 6 for example in [CS16]). For
example, let ct0 and ct1 be two ciphertexts. The worst-case approach then consists in
determining (possibly probabilistic) bounds B0 and B1 on ct0 and ct1 respectively. Let
ϵi = Bi −||⟨cti, sk⟩||∞, i ∈{0, 1}, the amount by which the bound deviates from the real
noise. The worst-case bound after an addition between ct0 and ct1 can then be calculated
from B0 and B1 as B = B0 + B1. This new bound deviates then by ϵ = ϵ0 + ϵ1 from the
real noise (i.e., the looseness has doubled). While such bounds are very safe, they are also
very loose in practice [CLP20], because the bounding error grows with the circuit depth.
Since loose bounds lead to an overly conservative choice of parameters, which in turn have
an impact on efficiency, we are interested in obtaining as tight bounds as possible.
The average-case analysis follows a different approach: instead of deriving a bound at
each step, we track the variance of the noise through every homomorphic computation,
and only derive a probabilistic bound at the very end.

4
Estimator
We implement a functional noise estimator whose goals are twofold: (i) to validate that our
theoretical noise estimations of Section 3 are correct and that they hold for a wide range
of large depth circuits with high accuracy and (ii) to experimentally, and independently
of the theoretical analysis, find the minimum amount of information that is necessary to
accurately track the noise.
As a result, and unlike previous noise estimations approaches, our estimator does not
track the variance of the message and noise through a single variable. Such an approach
works in the average case for basic operations, but it breaks down in practice when we
start to consider structured plaintexts or start to compose basic operations. Instead, and
similarly to how noise estimates are derived in Section 3, we experimentally concluded that
for an estimator to be accurate, it needs to track each and every coefficient of the message
and the noise components. The estimator therefore not only models how the noise evolves
during homomorphic operations, but also what the expected plaintext result would be.
This enables users to verify the correctness and behavior of an encrypted circuit, without
having to perform computations in the encrypted domain.
4.1
Internal Workings
The estimator models its homomorphic operations, and how they are performed,
on the implementation provided by the Lattigo library [Lat24].
It supports all the
elementary homomorphic operations, as well as some of the advanced ones, such as linear
transformations, homomorphic DFTs, polynomial evaluation and bootstrapping.
Unlike previous approaches, which operate on messages characterized by their dis-
tribution, our estimator requires the user to provide concrete messages. The estimator
then adds the expected encoding and encryption noise and operates on the message as it
would be done under encryption. Then, it updates the values throughout the user-defined
circuit. The message and noise are stored in the Canonical embedding for two reasons:
(i) arithmetic can be carried out as point-wise arithmetic over complex numbers and (ii)
we do not need to evaluate DFTs when multiplying elements. This approach enables all
linear noise propagation to be automatically and efficiently carried out, without requiring
approximations (e.g. addition or tensoring). The noise approximation is only introduced

when non-linear operations are called, such as the rescaling or key-switching, to ensure
that they remain efficient. During these operations, only the part that would modify the
plaintext is exact; the rest, for example how the noise is expected to evolve, is approximated.
We perform these approximations by sampling fresh noise according to the derivations of
Section 3 and performing an approximate mapping to the Canonical embedding by scaling
it by 1/

4.2
Performance
The current implementation of our estimator should be viewed as a proof of concept that
validates our approach, and not as a final product. It does not benefit from an optimized
implementation and in its current state it uses arbitrary precision complex arithmetic to
ensure that all computations are accurate, bringing it on par with the time necessary to
run the computation in the encrypted domain. We however believe that an optimized
implementation could significantly improve its efficiency, namely because most operations
in the estimator are Hadamard products or additions, and the most time-consuming
operation under encryption, the key-switching, is replaced in the estimator by a noise
sampling. Regardless, running the computation with the estimator requires a much lower
memory than running the computation in the encrypted domain since no evaluation keys
are needed and computations do not require to be carried out modulo a large prime.

5.4
Exact CKKS and IND-CPA-D Security
We can easily see that a (δ, 0)-exact CKKS scheme is IND-CPA-D secure if 1−δ is negligible.
There are common parameter sets such that 1 −δ is negligible. Choosing for example
n = 8192 and α = 14 results in a negligible δ, as does choosing α = 14 and n = 16384.
However, the above results do not directly give us IND-CPA-D security. The reason is that,
in order to bound the error in CKKS, we must approximate the distribution of the error by
a normal distribution – this is well founded, the central limit theorem indeed gives us that
the distribution converges towards a normal distribution, and from experimental evaluation
we know that this convergence is fast. However, the distribution is only approximately
Gaussian, and the actual distance from a normal distribution is hard to calculate. Thus,
we cannot say by how much the distribution fails to be normal. We know that if the
distribution is normal, the bounds hold with probability δ. But in order to calculate
the advantage an adversary has against the IND-CPA-D game, we also need to compute
the probability that the distribution fails to be normal, which would give us the (full)
probability that the bounds fail. This probability strongly depends on the circuit that is
evaluated, leading to circuit-specific intractable calculations. Experimentally, we know that
the probability that the distribution fails to behave in its tails like a normal distribution is
small. Thus, applying our procedure is likely to prevent IND-CPA-D attacks in practice.
However, formally this cannot be proven, since the complete failure probability is hard to
quantify. This problem can be circumvented by using worst-case bounds that hold with
probability 1: instead of making any assumptions about the distribution, the error term
can also be bounded by looking the absolute maximal value of each element in the error
term. However, these bounds are so large that applying them would also mean losing the
entire message.
6
Conclusion
In this work, we present tight average-case noise bounds for all basic operations in CKKS.
We show that our bounds are composable, thus allowing us to provide tight noise estimates
for complex homomorphic circuits. Additionally, we provide a tool – the estimator – that
allows us to illustrate how to combine our estimates for basic operations into estimates for
arbitrarily large circuits. Further, we provide experimental results showing the tightness
of our bounds. Given a circuit (such as binary value cleaning and bootstrapping), we run


J.-P. Bossuat, A. Costache, C. Mouchet, L. N¨urnberger, J. R. Troncoso-Pastoriza
23
it homomorphically, and we also run the estimator on it. Then, we compare the distance
between noise output of the former and the estimate output of the latter. We find that our
estimates deviate by less than 0.01 bits from the experimentally observed noise. Thus, we
provide the first tight noise analysis for CKKS bootstrapping, and more generally, the first
tight noise analysis for arbitrary circuits in CKKS. Additionally, we discuss an application
of our work: we show how our results can be used to obtain an exact version of the CKKS
scheme that preserves the efficiency advantages CKKS has over schemes such as BGV and
BFV. We additionally show how such an exact CKKS scheme is a step towards a practical
solution for achieving IND-CPA-D security for CKKS.

The steps of an (RNS-)CKKS bootstrapping can be summarized as follows. Let ct be
an RNS-CKKS ciphertext at the lowest level ℓ= 0, encrypting a plaintext pt.
1. Mod Raise In a first step the ciphertext is raised to a higher modulus QL, through
applying the map Rq0 →Rq0 × Rq1 × . . . × RqL. This map does not apply any
scaling to the ciphertext coefficients, but acts as an implicit decryption. Since this
decryption is done modulo QL and not Q0 = q0, the new ciphertext ct′ will now
encrypt pt + Iq0 where I is a small norm polynomial representing the q0 overflows
that were not removed. It will be the purpose of the subsequent 3 steps to evaluate
a reduction modulo q0 on ct′.
2. Coefficients to Slots The new message pt + Iq0 is in the coefficient format, thus does
not support slot-wise arithmetic. The message pt + Iq0 is therefore homomorphically
transformed from the coefficients to the slots format to allow for slot-wise evaluation
of the modulus reduction. The coefficients to slots algorithm is the same as the one
used to encode a message from the message space into the plaintext space (up to a
bit-reversal permutation), only that it is now evaluated homomorphically. This step
returns DFT−1(pt + Iq0).
3. Evaluate the Sine function The reduction modulo q0 is not a polynomial function and
cannot be easily evaluated homomorphically. It is approximated by a scaled sine
function, which in turn is approximated by its polynomial interpolation. This step
homomorphically evaluates the polynomial interpolation of the scaled sine function
on ct′, to obtain a ciphertext ct′′ encrypting only DFT−1(pt).
4. Slots to coefficients The ciphertext ct′′ is transformed back into the coefficients format
by homomorphically applying the decoding procedure, returning an encryption of
pt but at level ℓ> 0.
The steps 2,3, and 4 all add to the noise growth in the ciphertext and consume levels,
which is why the resulting bootstrapped ciphertext ct′′ may have slightly higher noise
than ct, and will be with respect to a level L−k where k is the depth of the bootstrapping
circuit. The precise growth of the noise is the subject of this work.

B.3
Noise Standard Deviation for Polynomial Evaluation
We proceed by giving expressions for the standard deviation that build up to a noise
estimate of the EvalMod1 Algorithm 6, which is the third step in the bootstrapping circuit.
The EvalMod1 algorithm consists of approximating the function fmod1 : x mod 1. Many
works have proposed solutions for this step [CHK+18, CCS19, LLK+22, LLL+21, LLKN20,
JM20, JM22, KPK+22]. We choose the approach of [HK20], as it provides in practice
the best overall performance in term of precision and depth consumption and is the
default approach in Lattigo. It approximates fmod1 with a phase-shifted scaled cosine
function, which enables an HE friendly evaluation of the double angle formula. The scaled
cosine function is itself approximated through polynomial interpolation using a powerful
basis consisting of Chebyshev polynomials. Afterwards, it calls the EvaluatePolynomial
algorithm, which evaluates the polynomial that has been interpolated to approximate
the fmod1 function. In this section, we give expressions for the standard deviation after
polynomial evaluation. We use the EvaluatePolynomial algorithm currently implemented
in Lattigo [Lat24] for our analysis and we recall it in Algorithm 7 in Appendix C.

Abstract: All RLWE-based FHE schemes are inherently noisy. The CKKS scheme (Cheon, Kim, Kim, Song, Asiacrypt 2017) considers the noise as a part of the message, yielding approximate computations but also considerable performance gains. Since it grows with each homomorphic operation and incurs a precision loss, it is paramount for users to be able to estimate the noise level throughout a given circuit in order to appropriately estimate parameters and control the precision loss in the message. In this work, we develop a noise model that allows for tight estimates of the precision loss, and propose a tool prototype for computing these estimates on any given circuit. Our noise model relies on a novel definition, the component-wise noise, which makes the average-case noise estimates tighter and more composable. As a result, our model and tool can derive accurate estimates of complex circuits such as bootstrapping. We experimentally demonstrate the tightness of our noise estimates by showing that our theoretical estimates never deviate by more than 0.01 bits from experimental estimates, even for large circuits, and hold with high probability. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to apply our techniques to obtain an exact version of the CKKS scheme in which the decryption removes all the noise (with high probability). Such a scheme has many applications, as it allows to take advantage of the efficiency of CKKS, while preserving an exact message space, hence further strengthening CKKS against IND-CPA-D attacks.
